title: Rethinking Asymmetry in Self-Supervised 3D Geometry Learning

paper.title: Rethinking Asymmetry in Self-Supervised 3D Geometry Learning
paper.abstract: Abstract Self-supervised learning relies on asymmetry between what a model observes and what it must explain. Recent methods learn 3D geometry from unposed images by predicting cameras and scene structure, then rendering held-out views. To avoid trivial solutions, they impose this asymmetry in the input space, restricting how views interact through separate branches or masked attention. We revisit this design with geometric accuracy, rather than rendering quality, as the main objective. When a held-out view lies between context views, the context already constrains the geometry it observes. We therefore impose the asymmetry in the 3D representation space, excluding held-out views only from the reconstructed scene while a shared backbone uses all views for correspondence. This improves depth and pose estimation over input-space designs. We further exploit view density: sparse and dense observations depict the same scene but provide different amounts of correspondence. Aligning sparse-context features with dense-context features supplies a geometric training signal alongside rendering, without a pretrained geometric teacher. We additionally align features with a frozen vision foundation model, which brings further gains. None of these signals requires geometric annotation, and the resulting model improves geometry estimation over prior self-supervised methods. Controlled experiments isolate the contribution of each component, and self-supervised pretraining also improves subsequent supervised training.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Self-supervised learning has driven the progress in representation learning. Because it requires no manual labels, models can be pretrained on as much data as we can collect, and their performance continues to improve as data, model size, and compute scale ( Kaplan et al., 2020 ) . This approach has succeeded in language ( Radford et al., 2018 ; Devlin et al., 2019 ) , vision ( Caron et al., 2021 ; He et al., 2022 ) , and embodied control ( Mu and Rhoda AI Team, 2026 ) . In contrast, many 3D foundation models are trained to reproduce geometric annotations recovered by optimization pipelines such as COLMAP ( Schönberger and Frahm, 2016 ) , which are costly to run and hard to scale. Recent work ( Jiang et al., 2025b ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2026b ) removes this dependence by making novel-view synthesis (NVS) the training objective, predicting cameras and scene structure from raw images or a video and rendering held-out views using its own predictions. These methods differ in scene representation and how they share information across views, but evaluations focus largely on synthesis quality. In self-supervised learning, however, the pretext task is only a means, and a method is judged by what it learns. We therefore treat view synthesis as the pretext and geometry as the outcome, and ask which designs make geometry learning more accurate and scalable. We begin with the scene representation. Since the model learns about the scene only through what it renders, the form of this representation determines how closely the learned structure reflects the actual 3D geometry. Latent NVS methods ( Jiang et al., 2025b ; Mitchel et al., 2026 ; Prestel et al., 2026 ) render held-out views from an implicit scene code, so geometry is never made explicit. They achieve strong rendering quality, but can do so without recovering structure that corresponds to physical 3D space, leaving geometry and camera motion only weakly constrained by the synthesis loss. We instead use an explicit representation, 3D Gaussians ( Kerbl et al., 2023 ) placed in physical space, so that every rendered pixel depends directly on the predicted depth and camera pose. Figure 2: All designs build the 3D scene from context views (C). (a) Separate backbones and (b) masked attention restrict interaction between context and held-out views (H). (c) Our design allows full cross-view attention while excluding held-out views from the 3D representation. Where should the asymmetry live? A self-supervised objective needs an asymmetry between what the model sees and what it must explain. Otherwise, trivial solutions satisfy it. For example, in masked image modeling ( He et al., 2022 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) , the image itself is the only place to create this asymmetry, so masking parts of it directly defines the task. In contrast, masking a view in multi-view 3D does not create the same asymmetry. When a held-out view lies between context views (interpolative NVS setting), the 3D scene reconstructed from the context views is the same scene that all views together describe. Removing the held-out view therefore hides nothing the model must recover. It only restricts the correspondence that would have helped recover that scene more accurately. Existing methods nevertheless impose the asymmetry on the images the network observes 1 1 1 This prevents held-out views from leaking into the reconstruction, which matters when rendering quality is the measure of interest. Geometry could also become biased toward the held-out views, but we find that richer view context in fact yields better geometric estimation (Sec. 3.2 ). . E-RayZer ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) splits camera and geometry prediction into two backbones so that the geometry branch sees only context views, and NAS3R ( Huang et al., 2026b ) masks view interaction between the context and held-out sets, so context views attend only among themselves. Both keep held-out views out of the reconstruction, but in doing so also withhold the correspondence those views could provide. We instead place the asymmetry in the 3D representation space. A shared backbone lets all views exchange information when predicting depth and pose, so every view contributes correspondence. We keep the context and held-out split of prior work but apply it when constructing the 3D scene, so that a held-out view is rendered only from Gaussians predicted for context views. This is equivalent to masking the 3D representation rather than the images. Every view thus informs correspondence estimation, while the self-reconstruction path is blocked. Asymmetric feature alignment. View density provides a second source of asymmetry. The same model predicts more accurate depth and pose when it sees more views of a scene, so a model given fewer views is a weaker version of itself. Such gaps within a single model have been used to bootstrap representations without any external teacher ( Jiang et al., 2025a ; Chefer et al., 2026 ) . SelfEvo ( Huang et al., 2026a ) applies this idea to 3D, refining a model pretrained with 3D supervision ( Wang et al., 2025b ; Wang et al., 2026c ) by using the geometry and camera predictions of a dense-context teacher as pseudo labels for a sparse-context student. We instead build this asymmetry into self-supervised training, optimizing it jointly with the rendering objective without any pretrained geometric teacher. In this setting the dense-context predictions are themselves unreliable, and matching them can propagate their errors. We therefore align the features that produce the geometry rather than the geometry itself. The largest gains occur in single-view depth estimation, which the rendering objective does not supervise directly. Semantics as a geometric prior. Both signals above are grounded in rendered pixels. The rendering loss supervises the model directly, and asymmetric context alignment does so indirectly through features shaped by rendering. Pixel agreement, however, says little about which pixels belong together, such as which regions form the same surface or object. Such high-level structure often helps constrain geometry where photometric cues are weak, such as textureless or repetitive regions. Vision foundation models capture it well, and aligning with their features has proven effective in generative modeling ( Yu et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2025 ) and supervised perception tasks ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Knaebel et al., 2026 ) . We use such alignment as a semantic prior for self-supervised learning, aligning our backbone features with those of a frozen vision foundation model ( Siméoni et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) , obtaining consistent gains in geometry estimation at modest additional cost. We combine these components into a single self-supervised geometry framework and evaluate each through controlled experiments. Our contributions are as follows. • Asymmetry in the 3D representation. We show that imposing the asymmetry on the reconstructed scene rather than on the input images prevents trivial solutions while letting a shared backbone use every view for correspondence, improving depth and pose estimation. • Asymmetric feature alignment. We align sparse-context features with dense-context features jointly with the rendering objective, improving geometry without a pretrained geometric teacher. • Semantics as a geometric prior. Aligning intermediate features with a frozen vision foundation model adds structural guidance beyond pixel agreement, improving depth and pose estimation without geometric annotations.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Self-supervised learning with novel-view synthesis. Feed-forward 3D models recover geometry directly from a set of images, but they are trained against camera and depth targets that an offline pipeline must produce first ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Wang et al., 2026c ; Lin et al., 2025 ) . A separate line of work has instead learned geometry from images alone. Early methods predicted depth and ego-motion from video and used warping between neighboring frames as supervision ( Zhou et al., 2017 ; Godard et al., 2019 ; Bian et al., 2019 ; Lai et al., 2021 ) , which ties learning to short baselines and pairwise constraints. RUST ( Sajjadi et al., 2023 ) and RayZer ( Jiang et al., 2025b ) removed explicit geometry altogether, encoding a scene into a latent set ( Sajjadi et al., 2022 ) and rendering new views with a learned decoder. Several methods extend this latent formulation to dynamic data and predictive (extrapolative) objectives ( Chen et al., 2026 ; Mitchel et al., 2026 ; Prestel et al., 2026 ) . Rendering in latent space minimizes inductive bias and lets the model learn freely from data, but it also leaves the recovered geometry only loosely tied to physical structure. Another line of work grounds the scene in 3D space and renders it by volume rendering or rasterization, jointly predicting poses and a NeRF ( Mildenhall et al., 2021 ) or Gaussian scene ( Kerbl et al., 2023 ) under photometric losses ( Chen and Lee, 2023 ; Fu et al., 2023 ; Kang et al., 2025 ) . Recently, E-RayZer ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) and NAS3R ( Huang et al., 2026b ) scaled explicit self-supervised reconstruction to large transformers and data, yielding representations with stronger geometric grounding. To prevent shortcuts and information leakage, both restrict how information moves between the context and held-out views, E-RayZer by separating camera and geometry prediction into two backbones, NAS3R by masking view interaction in its single backbone. The restriction keeps the objective from collapsing, but at the cost of rich correspondence. We instead investigate where this restriction should be placed, and find that the scene representation is a better location than the input. Self-supervised representation alignment. Aligning intermediate features to an additional target has become a common way to improve representation learning beyond what the task loss provides. In generative modeling, REPA ( Yu et al., 2024 ) and follow-up work ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Shin et al., 2026 ) align diffusion transformer features ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) with a frozen vision foundation model ( Oquab et al., 2023 ) , accelerating convergence and improving sample quality. Perception models use the same idea, aligning task features with such encoders ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Knaebel et al., 2026 ) or distilling several of them into one ( Ranzinger et al., 2024 ; Zhu et al., 2026 ) . On the other hand, recent work derives the target from the model itself, comparing its own representations across different inputs or layers ( Jiang et al., 2025a ; Chefer et al., 2026 ) . SelfEvo ( Huang et al., 2026a ) brings this to 3D, distilling a dense-context teacher into a sparse-context student, though it starts from a supervised model and aligns the two branches through their predicted depth. We exploit the same sparse-dense gap without 3D-supervised initialization, aligning features jointly with the main rendering objective during training. We also align them with a frozen vision encoder, providing complementary internal and external signals without geometric annotations.

sections.heading: 3.2 Asymmetry in the 3D Representation
sections.text: We now ask where the asymmetry should be placed when the goal is geometry rather than rendering. Prior designs keep target views out of view interaction so that the model cannot observe what it is asked to render. However, when a target view lies between context views, the context views already cover most of the geometry the target observes (Fig. 3 ), so the target contributes correspondence rather than new scene content. The asymmetry therefore only needs to prevent a target view from being rendered from its own prediction. It need not restrict which views interact. We test this against existing placements, holding the representation, encoder, and training setup fixed. Controlled comparison. We compare three placements of asymmetry. All variants share a visual encoder ( Yang et al., 2026 ) followed by a 12-layer transformer ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) with alternating view-wise and global attention ( Wang et al., 2025b ) . The full-view variant (ours) and the masked-attention variant predict cameras and Gaussians from this backbone. The separate-branch variant follows E-RayZer, predicting cameras from the backbone and Gaussians from a second 12-layer transformer, which gives it more capacity. All variants are trained on DL3DV ( Ling et al., 2024 ) for 100K iterations with the same data, view sampling, and optimization settings, with the number of views varying across training batches. At evaluation, we fix the frame span at 48 frames, so fewer views provide sparser coverage of the same scene (Fig. 4 ). Despite having less capacity than the separate-branch variant, the full-view variant achieves the most accurate depth and pose at every view count. Placing the asymmetry in the 3D representation rather than on interaction between views lets every view contribute correspondence while still blocking the self-reconstruction path. Figure 4: Effect of full interaction on depth and pose estimation. Depth is compared with MoGe-2 ( Wang et al., 2025c ) pseudo ground truth, and pose with dataset cameras.

sections.heading: 3.3 Beyond Rendering Signals
sections.text: Learning from context asymmetry. The preceding analysis shows that geometry estimates become less accurate as the view set becomes sparser. Dense and sparse predictions come from the same network on the same scene, so the gap reflects only what the extra views contribute, and this asymmetry can serve as a learning signal. SelfEvo ( Huang et al., 2026a ) turns this gap into supervision for a pretrained 3D foundation model ( Wang et al., 2025b ; Wang et al., 2026c ) , using the outputs of a dense-context teacher, maintained as an EMA of the model, as pseudo labels for a sparse-context student. We build on this idea with one key difference. Our model is trained entirely through self-supervision, with no 3D supervision to anchor its predictions. In this setting, depth predicted from different view sets shares no common scale, and the dense-context depth can itself be unreliable. In our experiments, distilling it directly degrades geometry even with a scale-invariant loss. We therefore move the alignment from the outputs to the features that produce them. These features carry the cross-view correspondence that dense context provides, but are not tied to a particular scale or depth value, making them a more stable target than the outputs they produce. We match them with a cosine similarity loss, which constrains their direction but leaves their magnitude free. sections.text: Our model is trained with three signals. The rendering loss defines the self-supervised task, asymmetric context alignment transfers dense-context features to sparse inputs, and semantic guidance injects a prior from a frozen foundation model. The total objective is ℒ = ℒ nvs + λ align ​ ℒ align + λ sem ​ ℒ sem , \mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{nvs}}+\lambda_{\text{align}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{align}}+\lambda_{\text{sem}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{sem}}, (5) where ℒ nvs \mathcal{L}_{\text{nvs}} combines an L2 and a perceptual loss ( Chen and Koltun, 2017 ) , and the λ \lambda terms balance the auxiliary losses against it. We set λ align = 0.1 \lambda_{\text{align}}=0.1 and λ sem = 0.2 \lambda_{\text{sem}}=0.2 . Since the dense-context features are only meaningful once rendering has shaped them, ℒ align \mathcal{L}_{\text{align}} is introduced at 40% of training and ramped to full weight by 60%.

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: Implementation details. Our model uses a pretrained Pixio (base) visual encoder ( Yang et al., 2026 ) followed by a 12-layer multi-view transformer with an alternating attention pattern, a feature dimension of 768 768 , and a 16 × \times 16 patch size. All experiments use this same backbone, which predicts both cameras and Gaussians. The camera head regresses each pose relative to the middle input view and predicts one set of intrinsics shared across the scene. A DPT head ( Ranftl et al., 2021 ; Wang et al., 2026b ) predicts per-pixel Gaussian attributes, which are lifted to 3D with the predicted cameras. The scene is built from context-view Gaussians only, and target views are rendered at their predicted poses by differentiable rasterization ( Kerbl et al., 2023 ) . Asymmetric context alignment uses the four transformer layers read by the DPT head, and semantic guidance uses the encoder output. Sparse subsets are formed by symmetrically dropping views on either side of the reference view, and the dense branch is an EMA copy of the online network with momentum 0.999. Datasets. We train separate models on RealEstate10K (RE10K) ( Zhou et al., 2018 ) and DL3DV ( Ling et al., 2024 ) , with images resized to 256 × 256 256\times 256 . ScanNetv2 ( Dai et al., 2017 ) and NRGBD ( Azinović et al., 2022 ) are used only for out-of-domain evaluation. Evaluation. We use publicly released baseline checkpoints and follow their evaluation settings. On RE10K, we adopt the view indices of SPFSplat ( Huang and Mikolajczyk, 2025 ) , and on DL3DV, we follow E-RayZer ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) and sample 10 views across a 96-frame span. For out-of-domain evaluation, we sample 10 views at a fixed stride, spanning 64 frames on ScanNetv2 and 256 on NRGBD. We report camera pose and depth, the two geometric quantities of interest. Camera pose is measured by relative pose accuracy (RPA) at several angular thresholds and by AUC@30. Depth is measured by AbsRel and threshold accuracy δ < 1.25 k \delta<1.25^{k} after independent per-view median alignment against ground-truth depth. Since DL3DV provides no ground-truth depth, our controlled analyses on DL3DV use MoGe-2 ( Wang et al., 2025c ) predictions as pseudo ground truth. Multi-view depth is predicted from the full input set, and single-view depth from each image alone. Depth conversion. All depth metrics use planar z z -depth. Our model and E-RayZer predict depth r r along each unit ray (Eq. 2 ), which we convert as z = r / ∥ K ^ − 1 ​ 𝐮 ∥ z=r/\lVert\hat{K}^{-1}\mathbf{u}\rVert using the predicted intrinsics K ^ \hat{K} , so focal-length errors are reflected in the depth metrics. For NAS3R, we use the z z -depth from its depth head. For SPFSplat, we transform its canonical point map into each view with the predicted pose and take the z z coordinate.

sections.heading: Single-image depth.
sections.text: We further evaluate depth when each frame is given to the model alone (Tab. 3 ). The network then receives only the reference camera token, so the pose head returns the identity pose together with a focal length predicted from the image, which we use to convert ray depth to z z -depth. Here our model outperforms E-RayZer on both datasets. Our multi-view depth is more accurate than our single-image depth on NRGBD, where our pose estimation is accurate, but less accurate on ScanNetv2, where pose estimation is much harder. The same pattern holds across scenes within ScanNetv2. When we sort the scenes by per-scene pose error and split them into three groups, multi-view depth outperforms single-image depth in 45% of the lowest-error scenes, 41% of the middle group, and only 3% of the highest-error scenes. Across all scenes, the multi-view AbsRel also increases with the pose error (Spearman ρ = 0.45 \rho=0.45 ). sections.text: We conduct controlled analyses on the DL3DV dataset to isolate the effect of each design choice. We investigate whether self-supervised learning improves subsequent supervised training, using the same architecture and data throughout. The supervised model (SL) is trained from scratch for 200K iterations with dataset camera poses and a relative camera loss ( Wang et al., 2026c ) . The self-supervised model (SSL) is trained without geometric supervision for 100K iterations. The fine-tuned model (SSL+SFT) starts from SSL and receives the same supervision as SL for another 50K iterations, for 150K iterations in total. sections.heading: 5 Discussion
sections.text: Design motivation. Prior pose-free methods restrict how held-out views enter the backbone, either by excluding them from geometry prediction or by preventing context views from attending to them. This choice is natural when rendering quality is the goal, since observing a held-out view could reveal what the model is asked to render. Our goal is geometry, with view synthesis serving only as the training signal. We keep the context and held-out split, but apply it to the 3D scene, so a held-out view is never rendered from its own prediction while still contributing correspondence in the shared backbone. For this reason, rendering metrics are not our primary basis of comparison. All designs receive the same images during training and differ only in how they use them. In restricted designs, held-out views cannot inform the context-view predictions from which the scene is built. In ours, every view informs every other. The gain therefore comes not from more data but from using the same views more effectively. Conclusion and future work. We study self-supervised geometry learning with rendering as the training objective and geometric accuracy as the outcome. Our central finding is that the asymmetry needed for self-supervision belongs in the 3D representation rather than in the network. Building on this, aligning sparse-context features with dense-context features turns view density into a further learning signal, and aligning with a frozen vision foundation model adds a semantic prior that pixels alone do not provide. Together, these choices form a simple design that improves camera pose and depth without geometric annotations. A key opportunity is to learn from visual data beyond annotation pipelines. Much of this data is casually captured monocular video, where the scene itself changes between frames, while our framework assumes a static scene. Our preliminary experiment suggests that the static model already tolerates some motion by assigning low opacity to moving content, which improves camera pose estimation on dynamic videos. This does not model motion, however, and moving objects are simply left out of the reconstruction. A natural next step can be an explicit dynamic representation that separates object motion from camera motion, either with Gaussians that move over time ( Wu et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2025 ) or with a separate reconstruction at each timestep in a bullet-time formulation ( Liang et al., 2024 ) . Such a representation offers a path toward self-supervised geometry learning from the far larger supply of monocular video.

sections.heading: A.1 Additional Details
sections.text: Training details. We train the main model for 100K iterations on RE10K ( Zhou et al., 2018 ) and 140K iterations on DL3DV ( Ling et al., 2024 ) on 8 NVIDIA B200 GPUs. The analysis variants are trained for 100K iterations on DL3DV on 2 NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs. Images are resized to 256 × 256 256\times 256 and tokenized with a patch size of 16, giving 256 tokens per view. Each batch uses a single view count from { 5 , 7 , 9 , 11 } \{5,7,9,11\} , split into ( N + 1 ) / 2 (N{+}1)/2 context and ( N − 1 ) / 2 (N{-}1)/2 target views, with per-device batch sizes of { 24 , 20 , 16 , 12 } \{24,20,16,12\} to keep the number of tokens per step roughly constant. Following RayZer ( Jiang et al., 2025b ) , we widen the frame span from which views are sampled over the first 80K iterations, moving from shorter to longer baselines, and keep it fixed afterward. The span grows from 24–96 to 48–192 frames on RE10K, from 24–48 to 32–54 on DL3DV, and from 24–32 to 32–48 for the analysis variants. We use AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017 ) with β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 , β 2 = 0.95 \beta_{2}=0.95 , and weight decay 0.05 0.05 , together with a cosine schedule and 3000 warm-up steps. The learning rate is 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} for the main model and 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} for the analysis variants. Training uses bf16 and FlashAttention-2 ( Dao, 2024 ) , with gradients clipped to a norm of 1.0 1.0 . Evaluation details. We evaluate on 5,601 RE10K scenes ( Zhou et al., 2018 ) , 140 DL3DV scenes ( Ling et al., 2024 ) , 9 NRGBD scenes ( Azinović et al., 2022 ) , and 97 ScanNetv2 scenes ( Dai et al., 2017 ) . We evaluate SPFSplat and NAS3R with their official evaluation code, which applies no masking at test time. In this comparison, depth is predicted and scored on all input views for both the baselines and our model. For E-RayZer, poses are estimated from all images and depth from the context views only. Accordingly, when comparing with E-RayZer, our DPT head decodes only the context views, and depth is scored on the same context views for both methods. Architecture. Fig. 12 illustrates the pipeline. A visual encoder tokenizes each view, and a learnable camera token is prepended to its patch tokens. Tokens from both context (C) and held-out (H) views enter a unified estimator with alternating view-wise and global attention, so every view can interact with every other. The resulting patch tokens feed a DPT head ( Ranftl et al., 2021 ) , which reads four intermediate estimator layers to predict per-pixel depth and the remaining Gaussian attributes. The camera tokens feed a relative pose head, which regresses each pose relative to the middle input view. Context-view depths are unprojected with the predicted cameras to form the Gaussian scene, which is then rendered at the predicted held-out poses. Since the asymmetry is imposed in the 3D representation, attention in the estimator remains unrestricted. Figure 12: Overall architecture, with a shared backbone for camera and geometry prediction.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY-SA 4.0 arXiv:2610.42092v1 [cs.CV] 30 Oct 2026 Rethinking Asymmetry in Self-Supervised 3D Geometry Learning Gyeongjin Kang Freeman Cheng Botao Ye Weijie Lyu Ming-Hsuan Yang Eunbyung Park Yonsei University UC Merced ETH Zurich Website Code Abstract Self-supervised learning relies on asymmetry between what a model observes and what it must explain. Recent methods learn 3D geometry from unposed images by predicting cameras and scene structure, then rendering held-out views. To avoid trivial solutions, they impose this asymmetry in the input space, restricting how views interact through separate branches or masked attention. We revisit this design with geometric accuracy, rather than rendering quality, as the main objective. When a held-out view lies between context views, the context already constrains the geometry it observes. We therefore impose the asymmetry in the 3D representation space, excluding held-out views only from the reconstructed scene while a shared backbone uses all views for correspondence. This improves depth and pose estimation over input-space designs. We further exploit view density: sparse and dense observations depict the same scene but provide different amounts of correspondence. Aligning sparse-context features with dense-context features supplies a geometric training signal alongside rendering, without a pretrained geometric teacher. We additionally align features with a frozen vision foundation model, which brings further gains. None of these signals requires geometric annotation, and the resulting model improves geometry estimation over prior self-supervised methods. Controlled experiments isolate the contribution of each component, and self-supervised pretraining also improves subsequent supervised training. Figure 1: From unposed images alone, our self-supervised model recovers camera poses and 3D geometry in a single forward pass (top), generalizes to unseen datasets, improves pose accuracy over baseline models (bottom left, middle), and provides an effective initialization for supervised fine-tuning (SSL+SFT), compared to supervised training only (bottom right). 1 Introduction Self-supervised learning has driven the progress in representation learning. Because it requires no manual labels, models can be pretrained on as much data as we can collect, and their performance continues to improve as data, model size, and compute scale ( Kaplan et al., 2020 ) . This approach has succeeded in language ( Radford et al., 2018 ; Devlin et al., 2019 ) , vision ( Caron et al., 2021 ; He et al., 2022 ) , and embodied control ( Mu and Rhoda AI Team, 2026 ) . In contrast, many 3D foundation models are trained to reproduce geometric annotations recovered by optimization pipelines such as COLMAP ( Schönberger and Frahm, 2016 ) , which are costly to run and hard to scale. Recent work ( Jiang et al., 2025b ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2026b ) removes this dependence by making novel-view synthesis (NVS) the training objective, predicting cameras and scene structure from raw images or a video and rendering held-out views using its own predictions. These methods differ in scene representation and how they share information across views, but evaluations focus largely on synthesis quality. In self-supervised learning, however, the pretext task is only a means, and a method is judged by what it learns. We therefore treat view synthesis as the pretext and geometry as the outcome, and ask which designs make geometry learning more accurate and scalable. We begin with the scene representation. Since the model learns about the scene only through what it renders, the form of this representation determines how closely the learned structure reflects the actual 3D geometry. Latent NVS methods ( Jiang et al., 2025b ; Mitchel et al., 2026 ; Prestel et al., 2026 ) render held-out views from an implicit scene code, so geometry is never made explicit. They achieve strong rendering quality, but can do so without recovering structure that corresponds to physical 3D space, leaving geometry and camera motion only weakly constrained by the synthesis loss. We instead use an explicit representation, 3D Gaussians ( Kerbl et al., 2023 ) placed in physical space, so that every rendered pixel depends directly on the predicted depth and camera pose. Figure 2: All designs build the 3D scene from context views (C). (a) Separate backbones and (b) masked attention restrict interaction between context and held-out views (H). (c) Our design allows full cross-view attention while excluding held-out views from the 3D representation. Where should the asymmetry live? A self-supervised objective needs an asymmetry between what the model sees and what it must explain. Otherwise, trivial solutions satisfy it. For example, in masked image modeling ( He et al., 2022 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) , the image itself is the only place to create this asymmetry, so masking parts of it directly defines the task. In contrast, masking a view in multi-view 3D does not create the same asymmetry. When a held-out view lies between context views (interpolative NVS setting), the 3D scene reconstructed from the context views is the same scene that all views together describe. Removing the held-out view therefore hides nothing the model must recover. It only restricts the correspondence that would have helped recover that scene more accurately. Existing methods nevertheless impose the asymmetry on the images the network observes 1 1 1 This prevents held-out views from leaking into the reconstruction, which matters when rendering quality is the measure of interest. Geometry could also become biased toward the held-out views, but we find that richer view context in fact yields better geometric estimation (Sec. 3.2 ). . E-RayZer ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) splits camera and geometry prediction into two backbones so that the geometry branch sees only context views, and NAS3R ( Huang et al., 2026b ) masks view interaction between the context and held-out sets, so context views attend only among themselves. Both keep held-out views out of the reconstruction, but in doing so also withhold the correspondence those views could provide. We instead place the asymmetry in the 3D representation space. A shared backbone lets all views exchange information when predicting depth and pose, so every view contributes correspondence. We keep the context and held-out split of prior work but apply it when constructing the 3D scene, so that a held-out view is rendered only from Gaussians predicted for context views. This is equivalent to masking the 3D representation rather than the images. Every view thus informs correspondence estimation, while the self-reconstruction path is blocked. Asymmetric feature alignment. View density provides a second source of asymmetry. The same model predicts more accurate depth and pose when it sees more views of a scene, so a model given fewer views is a weaker version of itself. Such gaps within a single model have been used to bootstrap representations without any external teacher ( Jiang et al., 2025a ; Chefer et al., 2026 ) . SelfEvo ( Huang et al., 2026a ) applies this idea to 3D, refining a model pretrained with 3D supervision ( Wang et al., 2025b ; Wang et al., 2026c ) by using the geometry and camera predictions of a dense-context teacher as pseudo labels for a sparse-context student. We instead build this asymmetry into self-supervised training, optimizing it jointly with the rendering objective without any pretrained geometric teacher. In this setting the dense-context predictions are themselves unreliable, and matching them can propagate their errors. We therefore align the features that produce the geometry rather than the geometry itself. The largest gains occur in single-view depth estimation, which the rendering objective does not supervise directly. Semantics as a geometric prior. Both signals above are grounded in rendered pixels. The rendering loss supervises the model directly, and asymmetric context alignment does so indirectly through features shaped by rendering. Pixel agreement, however, says little about which pixels belong together, such as which regions form the same surface or object. Such high-level structure often helps constrain geometry where photometric cues are weak, such as textureless or repetitive regions. Vision foundation models capture it well, and aligning with their features has proven effective in generative modeling ( Yu et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2025 ) and supervised perception tasks ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Knaebel et al., 2026 ) . We use such alignment as a semantic prior for self-supervised learning, aligning our backbone features with those of a frozen vision foundation model ( Siméoni et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) , obtaining consistent gains in geometry estimation at modest additional cost. We combine these components into a single self-supervised geometry framework and evaluate each through controlled experiments. Our contributions are as follows. • Asymmetry in the 3D representation. We show that imposing the asymmetry on the reconstructed scene rather than on the input images prevents trivial solutions while letting a shared backbone use every view for correspondence, improving depth and pose estimation. • Asymmetric feature alignment. We align sparse-context features with dense-context features jointly with the rendering objective, improving geometry without a pretrained geometric teacher. • Semantics as a geometric prior. Aligning intermediate features with a frozen vision foundation model adds structural guidance beyond pixel agreement, improving depth and pose estimation without geometric annotations. 2 Related Work Self-supervised learning with novel-view synthesis. Feed-forward 3D models recover geometry directly from a set of images, but they are trained against camera and depth targets that an offline pipeline must produce first ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Wang et al., 2026c ; Lin et al., 2025 ) . A separate line of work has instead learned geometry from images alone. Early methods predicted depth and ego-motion from video and used warping between neighboring frames as supervision ( Zhou et al., 2017 ; Godard et al., 2019 ; Bian et al., 2019 ; Lai et al., 2021 ) , which ties learning to short baselines and pairwise constraints. RUST ( Sajjadi et al., 2023 ) and RayZer ( Jiang et al., 2025b ) removed explicit geometry altogether, encoding a scene into a latent set ( Sajjadi et al., 2022 ) and rendering new views with a learned decoder. Several methods extend this latent formulation to dynamic data and predictive (extrapolative) objectives ( Chen et al., 2026 ; Mitchel et al., 2026 ; Prestel et al., 2026 ) . Rendering in latent space minimizes inductive bias and lets the model learn freely from data, but it also leaves the recovered geometry only loosely tied to physical structure. Another line of work grounds the scene in 3D space and renders it by volume rendering or rasterization, jointly predicting poses and a NeRF ( Mildenhall et al., 2021 ) or Gaussian scene ( Kerbl et al., 2023 ) under photometric losses ( Chen and Lee, 2023 ; Fu et al., 2023 ; Kang et al., 2025 ) . Recently, E-RayZer ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) and NAS3R ( Huang et al., 2026b ) scaled explicit self-supervised reconstruction to large transformers and data, yielding representations with stronger geometric grounding. To prevent shortcuts and information leakage, both restrict how information moves between the context and held-out views, E-RayZer by separating camera and geometry prediction into two backbones, NAS3R by masking view interaction in its single backbone. The restriction keeps the objective from collapsing, but at the cost of rich correspondence. We instead investigate where this restriction should be placed, and find that the scene representation is a better location than the input. Self-supervised representation alignment. Aligning intermediate features to an additional target has become a common way to improve representation learning beyond what the task loss provides. In generative modeling, REPA ( Yu et al., 2024 ) and follow-up work ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Shin et al., 2026 ) align diffusion transformer features ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) with a frozen vision foundation model ( Oquab et al., 2023 ) , accelerating convergence and improving sample quality. Perception models use the same idea, aligning task features with such encoders ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Knaebel et al., 2026 ) or distilling several of them into one ( Ranzinger et al., 2024 ; Zhu et al., 2026 ) . On the other hand, recent work derives the target from the model itself, comparing its own representations across different inputs or layers ( Jiang et al., 2025a ; Chefer et al., 2026 ) . SelfEvo ( Huang et al., 2026a ) brings this to 3D, distilling a dense-context teacher into a sparse-context student, though it starts from a supervised model and aligns the two branches through their predicted depth. We exploit the same sparse-dense gap without 3D-supervised initialization, aligning features jointly with the main rendering objective during training. We also align them with a frozen vision encoder, providing complementary internal and external signals without geometric annotations. 3 Approach 3.1 Preliminaries Setup. Where asymmetry is placed. Existing methods keep target views out of the reconstructed scene by restricting how information flows between views. Separate branches ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) predict cameras from all views but geometry from context views alone, using separate features without the interaction that a shared representation can provide. Held-out views add correspondence, not new geometry. 3.2 Asymmetry in the 3D Representation We now ask where the asymmetry should be placed when the goal is geometry rather than rendering. Prior designs keep target views out of view interaction so that the model cannot observe what it is asked to render. However, when a target view lies between context views, the context views already cover most of the geometry the target observes (Fig. 3 ), so the target contributes correspondence rather than new scene content. The asymmetry therefore only needs to prevent a target view from being rendered from its own prediction. It need not restrict which views interact. We test this against existing placements, holding the representation, encoder, and training setup fixed. Controlled comparison. We compare three placements of asymmetry. The preceding analysis shows that geometry estimates become less accurate as the view set becomes sparser. Dense and sparse predictions come from the same network on the same scene, so the gap reflects only what the extra views contribute, and this asymmetry can serve as a learning signal. SelfEvo ( Huang et al., 2026a ) turns this gap into supervision for a pretrained 3D foundation model ( Wang et al., 2025b ; Wang et al., 2026c ) , using the outputs of a dense-context teacher, maintained as an EMA of the model, as pseudo labels for a sparse-context student. We build on this idea with one key difference. Our model is trained entirely through self-supervision, with no 3D supervision to anchor its predictions. Prior pose-free methods restrict how held-out views enter the backbone, either by excluding them from geometry prediction or by preventing context views from attending to them. This choice is natural when rendering quality is the goal, since observing a held-out view could reveal what the model is asked to render. Our goal is geometry, with view synthesis serving only as the training signal. We keep the context and held-out split, but apply it to the 3D scene, so a held-out view is never rendered from its own prediction while still contributing correspondence in the shared backbone. For this reason, rendering metrics are not our primary basis of comparison. All designs receive the same images during training and differ only in how they use them. In restricted designs, held-out views cannot inform the context-view predictions from which the scene is built. In ours, every view informs every other. The gain therefore comes not from more data but from using the same views more effectively. Conclusion and future work. We study self-supervised geometry learning with rendering as the training objective and geometric accuracy as the outcome. Our central finding is that the asymmetry needed for self-supervision belongs in the 3D representation rather than in the network. Building on this, aligning sparse-context features with dense-context features turns view density into a further learning signal, and aligning with a frozen vision foundation model adds a semantic prior that pixels alone do not provide. Together, these choices form a simple design that improves camera pose and depth without geometric annotations. A key opportunity is to learn from visual data beyond annotation pipelines. Much of this data is casually captured monocular video, where the scene itself changes between frames, while our framework assumes a static scene.
